intent: Eight individual modal and quantity tasks preserve suggestion, advice, amount/count, capacity, negative few, equal-sheet paper amount and bounded steep-step comparison.
picturePurpose: Exact coded paper sheets and path steps are the visual explanation. Original statements remain separate from stipulated exercise counts; no generated image can supply unknown measurements or past attention.

transfer.stem: Which report keeps the comparisons and question meaning correct?
transfer.passage:
Checking our model-making report
Our club was planning a display. “Shall we try the shorter route?” was a suggestion, not a final decision about how to get there. We ought to leave time for questions at the display; this did not mean the time had already been set aside.
We checked two questions carefully. “How much water does this plant need?” asked about an amount of water, not a number of bottles. “How many boxes can the shelf hold?” asked about capacity, not just the boxes already on the shelf. Neither question supplied its own numerical answer.
A note said that few people had noticed a tiny sign. We kept the sense of a very small number, without inventing an exact count of zero. Another note said that our design used less paper. That concerned the amount of paper, not a claim that every sheet was smaller. In a separate practice model we used equal-sized sheets and made one finished object with each design. Only then did comparing sheet counts also compare the amount of paper.
The new route had fewer steep steps. This compared the number of steep steps, not the steepness of each step or the route’s distance. We still needed more time to test the display idea. That was a need for additional testing time, not a report that testing was finished.

options.text: The shelf question asks about capacity; less paper concerns an amount; fewer steep steps does not prove a shorter distance.
The shelf question asks only about boxes already on it; less paper concerns an amount; fewer steep steps does not prove a shorter distance.
The shelf question asks about capacity; less paper proves that each sheet is smaller; fewer steep steps does not prove a shorter distance.
The shelf question asks about capacity; less paper concerns an amount; fewer steep steps proves a shorter distance.
